entries.lesson_core_move: Identify the nonzero interval of $x(\tau)$ in the convolution variable so it becomes the fixed support constraint for determining overlap with $h(t-\tau)$.

sections.section_title: Introduction to Finding the Support of $x(\tau)$

blocks.text: In a convolution integral, $\tau$ is the integration variable. The value of $t$ is treated as fixed later, but the first support constraint comes only from the signal $x(\tau)$.
The support of $x(\tau)$ means the set of $\tau$ values where $x(\tau)$ is nonzero. To find it, ignore $h(t-\tau)$ for now and read only where the input-side signal is active.
For the cleanest case, suppose $x(\tau)$ is equal to $1$ on one interval and is $0$ everywhere else. The support is exactly the interval where the nonzero branch appears.

So the fixed support constraint from $x(\tau)$ is $0\le \tau\le 2$. It is fixed because it depends only on $x(\tau)$ and contains no $t$; later overlap work will combine this fixed constraint with the moving support of $h(t-\tau)$.

sections.section_title: Reading the Support of a Basic Signal in $\tau$

example_content.example_prompt: Find the support of $x(\tau)$ if $x(\tau)=2$ for $-1\le \tau\le 3$ and $x(\tau)=0$ otherwise.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is the phrase that tells us exactly when $x(\tau)$ is nonzero. Here, $x(\tau)=2$ on $-1\le \tau\le 3$, so the amplitude $2$ only tells us the signal is active on that interval.
Everywhere outside that interval, the signal is given as $0$, so those $\tau$ values are not part of the support. The support is the interval from the nonzero clause.
So the fixed support constraint for this signal is $-1\le \tau\le 3$. This constraint comes only from $x(\tau)$; no comparison with $h(t-\tau)$ is needed in this step.

sections.section_title: Finding Support from a Piecewise Definition in $\tau$

example_content.example_prompt: Find the support of $x(\tau)=\begin{cases}0,&\tau<-1\\\tau+3,&-1\le \tau\le 2\\0,&\tau>2\end{cases}$.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is the piecewise definition. To find the support, scan the branches and separate the branches where $x(\tau)$ is exactly $0$ from the branch where $x(\tau)$ is nonzero.
The first branch is zero for $\tau<-1$, and the last branch is zero for $\tau>2$. Those intervals are not part of the support.
The remaining branch is $x(\tau)=\tau+3$ on $-1\le \tau\le 2$. This is the active branch, so its condition gives the support interval.
So the fixed support constraint for this signal is $-1\le \tau\le 2$. This step uses only the branches of $x(\tau)$; it does not involve $h(t-\tau)$ or any overlap calculation.

sections.section_title: Finding Support from Unit Step Windows in $\tau$

example_content.example_prompt: Find the support of $x(\tau)=(u(\tau-1)-u(\tau-4))e^{-\tau}$.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is the unit-step difference $u(\tau-1)-u(\tau-4)$. This factor acts like a window: it turns the signal on at one $\tau$ value and turns it off at another.
The term $u(\tau-1)$ turns on at $\tau=1$. The subtracted term $u(\tau-4)$ turns on at $\tau=4$, which turns the window off after that point.
The multiplier $e^{-\tau}$ does not create a new cutoff because it is nonzero for every $\tau$. So the support comes from the unit-step window.
So the fixed support constraint for this signal is $1\le \tau\le 4$. This is still a constraint from $x(\tau)$ only; no overlap with $h(t-\tau)$ is being formed yet.

sections.section_title: Writing the Fixed Support Constraint for $x(\tau)$

example_content.example_prompt: Given that $x(\tau)$ is nonzero only for $-2\le \tau\le 1$, write the fixed support constraint for $x(\tau)$ that will be used later when finding overlap with $h(t-\tau)$.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is that the nonzero interval for $x(\tau)$ has already been identified. Since $x(\tau)$ is nonzero only for $-2\le \tau\le 1$, that interval is the support of $x$.
To write this as a support constraint, keep the convolution variable $\tau$ in the inequality and copy the support endpoints in increasing order.
This constraint is fixed because it contains no $t$. It comes only from $x(\tau)$, so it does not move as the output time changes.
Later overlap work will combine this fixed constraint with the support of $h(t-\tau)$. For this step, stop here and do not form an intersection.

entries.lesson_core_move: Convert the support interval of $h(u)$ into the corresponding interval for $h(t-\tau)$ by holding $t$ fixed and reversing the inequalities in $\tau$.

sections.section_title: Introduction to Finding the Support of $h(t-\tau)$

blocks.text: In convolution, the support of $x(\tau)$ is a fixed interval in the variable $\tau$. The support of $h(t-\tau)$ is different: for each held value of $t$, we need the set of $\tau$ values that make the argument of $h$ land inside the support of $h$.

Use $u$ as a temporary name for the input to $h$. Since the input to $h(t-\tau)$ is $u=t-\tau$, the rule is: put $t-\tau$ into the known support condition for $h(u)$, treat $t$ as a constant, and solve for $\tau$.

blocks.latex: h(u) \ne 0 \text{ for } 0 \le u \le a \quad\Longrightarrow\quad h(t-\tau) \ne 0 \text{ when } 0 \le t-\tau \le a

blocks.text: Now isolate $\tau$. The important algebraic detail is that $\tau$ has a negative sign in $t-\tau$, so multiplying by $-1$ reverses both inequality directions.

blocks.latex: \begin{aligned} 0 &\le t-\tau \le a \\ -t &\le -\tau \le a-t \\ t &\ge \tau \ge t-a \\ t-a &\le \tau \le t \end{aligned}

blocks.text: So if $h(u)$ is supported on $0\le u\le a$, then $h(t-\tau)$ is supported on $t-a\le \tau\le t$. The output of this step is an increasing interval in $\tau$; later, that interval can be compared with the fixed support of $x(\tau)$.

sections.section_title: Holding $t$ Fixed in the Support Condition for $h(t-\tau)$

example_content.example_prompt: Suppose $h(u)$ is nonzero for $0 \le u \le 3$. For fixed $t=5$, find the support of $h(t-\tau)$ in terms of $\tau$.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is the expression $h(t-\tau)$ together with a fixed value of $t$. Since $t=5$, the argument of $h$ is $5-\tau$, and $h(5-\tau)$ is nonzero exactly when that argument lies in the support of $h(u)$.
Replace $u$ with $5-\tau$ because the input to $h$ is now $5-\tau$.
Now solve this compound inequality for $\tau$. Subtract $5$ from each part, then multiply by $-1$; multiplying by $-1$ reverses the inequality directions.
So, for fixed $t=5$, the support of $h(t-\tau)$ is $2\le \tau\le 5$. This is the moving-support interval after substituting this particular value of $t$, not an overlap interval yet.

sections.section_title: Converting an $h(u)$ Support Interval into an Inequality for $t-\tau$

example_content.example_prompt: Suppose $h(u)$ is nonzero for $1 \le u \le 4$. Write the support condition for $h(t-\tau)$ before isolating $\tau$.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is that the known support is written for $h(u)$, but the signal in the convolution is $h(t-\tau)$. That means the input to $h$ is no longer $u$; the input is $t-\tau$.
The support endpoints stay the same because $h$ is nonzero when its argument lands between $1$ and $4$. So replace only the argument $u$ with $t-\tau$.

So the support condition for $h(t-\tau)$, before isolating $\tau$, is $1\le t-\tau\le 4$. This section stops here: solving that inequality for $\tau$ is the next move, not part of this conversion step.

sections.section_title: Reversing Inequalities to Isolate $\tau$

example_content.example_prompt: Given that $2 \le t-\tau \le 6$, isolate $\tau$ and write the support interval for $h(t-\tau)$.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is that the support condition has already been converted into an inequality involving $t-\tau$. Now the task is only to solve that inequality for $\tau$, treating $t$ as fixed.
First subtract $t$ from all three parts so that $-\tau$ is alone in the middle.
Now multiply all three parts by $-1$. Because this multiplication uses a negative number, both inequality signs reverse.
The values of $\tau$ are usually written from the smaller endpoint to the larger endpoint, so rewrite the same interval in increasing $\tau$ order.
Therefore, the support interval for $h(t-\tau)$ is $t-6\le \tau\le t-2$. The key algebraic move was reversing the inequalities when $-\tau$ became $\tau$.

sections.section_title: Writing the $h(t-\tau)$ Support Interval in Increasing $\tau$ Order

example_content.example_prompt: Suppose $h(u)$ is nonzero for $-2 \le u \le 3$. Find the support of $h(t-\tau)$ and write it in increasing $\tau$ order.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is the support interval for $h(u)$ together with the shifted argument $t-\tau$. First convert the $h(u)$ support into a condition on the argument of $h(t-\tau)$.
Now isolate $\tau$. Subtract $t$ from all three parts so that $-\tau$ is in the middle.
Multiply by $-1$ and reverse both inequality signs. This gives the correct endpoints, but the interval is now written in decreasing $\tau$ order.
Compare the two endpoint expressions. Since $t-3$ is smaller than $t+2$, write $t-3$ on the left and $t+2$ on the right.
Therefore, the support of $h(t-\tau)$ is $t-3\le \tau\le t+2$. Writing the smaller $\tau$ endpoint first keeps the moving support ready for later overlap comparisons.

sections.section_title: Checking the Moving Support Interval Against the Flip-Shift Picture

image_slots.image_description: Create a sparse instructional support-interval diagram with two stacked horizontal axes. The top axis is labeled u and shows h(u) nonzero on a shaded interval from u=0 to u=2, with endpoints 0 and 2 marked. The bottom axis is labeled tau and shows h(t-\tau) for fixed t on a shaded interval from tau=t-2 to tau=t, with endpoints t-2 and t marked. Include a small label 't fixed'. Add simple annotations showing that u=2 maps to tau=t-2 and u=0 maps to tau=t, so the endpoint order reverses because the argument is t-\tau. Do not include x(\tau), overlap regions, integral bounds, amplitudes, decorative elements, or extra axes.

example_content.example_prompt: Use the flip-shift picture to check the support interval of $h(t-\tau)$ when $h(u)$ is nonzero on $0 \le u \le 2$.

explanation_blocks.text: The picture should confirm the symbolic support result, not replace it. Start by reading the original support endpoints from the $u$-axis: $h(u)$ is nonzero from $u=0$ to $u=2$.
Using the symbolic rule from the previous sections, place the argument $t-\tau$ inside the original support interval and solve for $\tau$.

The flip-shift picture matches that result. The right endpoint of the original $u$ support, $u=2$, becomes the left endpoint $\tau=t-2$, and the left endpoint $u=0$ becomes the right endpoint $\tau=t$.

Therefore, the pictured moving support confirms the increasing-$\tau$ interval $t-2\le \tau\le t$. This check is only about the support of $h(t-\tau)$; it does not yet compare against $x(\tau)$ or set integration bounds.

entries.lesson_core_move: Intersect the support of $x(\tau)$ with the support of $h(t-\tau)$ for a fixed $t$ to determine where the convolution integrand is nonzero.

sections.section_title: Introduction to Determining the Overlap Interval

blocks.text: In the previous lessons, you found the support of $x(\tau)$ and the support of $h(t-\tau)$ separately. The next move is to combine those two support intervals in the convolution variable $\tau$.
The product $x(\tau)h(t-\tau)$ can be nonzero only at values of $\tau$ where both factors are nonzero at the same time. That common set of $\tau$ values is called the overlap interval.

For example, suppose $x(\tau)$ is nonzero on $0\le \tau\le 2$, and $h(t-\tau)$ is nonzero on $t-3\le \tau\le t-1$. While finding overlap, treat $t$ as fixed and decide which $\tau$ values satisfy both interval conditions.
In general, the left endpoint of the overlap comes from the larger lower endpoint, and the right endpoint comes from the smaller upper endpoint.

blocks.latex: \text{If the supports are } [a,b] \text{ and } [c(t),d(t)], \text{ then overlap is } [\max(a,c(t)),\min(b,d(t))].

blocks.text: Later sections will compare these endpoints to find the actual overlap interval in each time region. For now, the key rule is: overlap means the intersection of the fixed support of $x(\tau)$ and the moving support of $h(t-\tau)$, with $t$ held fixed.

sections.section_title: Intersecting Supports for One Fixed $t$

example_content.example_prompt: Suppose $x(\tau)$ is nonzero on $0 \le \tau \le 4$ and $h(t-\tau)$ is nonzero on $t-3 \le \tau \le t-1$. Determine the overlap interval when $t=5$.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is the fixed value $t=5$. First substitute that value into the moving support interval for $h(t-\tau)$.
Now compare this moving support with the fixed support of $x(\tau)$.
The overlap interval must satisfy both support conditions. Use the larger lower endpoint and the smaller upper endpoint.
Since the lower endpoint $2$ is not greater than the upper endpoint $4$, the interval is nonempty. The overlap interval when $t=5$ is $2 \le \tau \le 4$.

sections.section_title: Writing Overlap with Lower and Upper Endpoint Rules

example_content.example_prompt: Suppose $x(\tau)$ is nonzero on $0 \le \tau \le 4$ and $h(t-\tau)$ is nonzero on $t-3 \le \tau \le t-1$. Write the overlap interval using lower- and upper-endpoint rules.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is that no numerical value of $t$ is given. Instead of substituting for $t$, keep the endpoints symbolic and use the endpoint rule for intersecting intervals.
The lower endpoint of the overlap must be at least as large as both lower endpoints. The two lower endpoints are $0$ and $t-3$, so the overlap starts at their maximum.
The upper endpoint of the overlap must be no larger than both upper endpoints. The two upper endpoints are $4$ and $t-1$, so the overlap ends at their minimum.
Therefore, the symbolic overlap interval is written by placing the maximum lower endpoint on the left and the minimum upper endpoint on the right.

This endpoint-rule interval applies on values of $t$ where the lower endpoint is not greater than the upper endpoint. Do not split it into cases yet; the goal here is only to record the overlap in max/min form.

sections.section_title: Finding the $t$ Values Where Endpoint Order Changes

example_content.example_prompt: For the endpoint-rule overlap $\max(0,t-3) \le \tau \le \min(4,t-1)$, find the $t$ values where the lower endpoint choice or upper endpoint choice can change.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is the endpoint-rule form. A chosen endpoint can change only when the two expressions competing inside the same $\max$ or $\min$ become equal.
For the lower endpoint, the competing expressions inside the maximum are $0$ and $t-3$. Set them equal to find where the lower endpoint choice can switch.
For the upper endpoint, the competing expressions inside the minimum are $4$ and $t-1$. Set them equal to find where the upper endpoint choice can switch.
List the switch values in increasing order. These are only the possible endpoint-change values; they are not yet a full piecewise overlap description.

sections.section_title: Determining Overlap Intervals Across Time Regions

example_content.example_prompt: For the active overlap range $1 \le t \le 7$, suppose the endpoint-rule overlap is $\max(0,t-3) \le \tau \le \min(4,t-1)$. Determine the overlap interval in each time region where the endpoint formulas differ.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is the active overlap range together with the endpoint-rule expression. The endpoint choices can change at $t=3$ and $t=5$, so use those values to split the active range.
On the first region, $1\le t\le 3$. The larger lower endpoint is $0$ because $t-3\le 0$, and the smaller upper endpoint is $t-1$ because $t-1\le 4$.
On the middle region, $3\le t\le 5$. Now $t-3$ is the larger lower endpoint, while $t-1$ is still the smaller upper endpoint.
On the final region, $5\le t\le 7$. The lower endpoint remains $t-3$, but the smaller upper endpoint is now $4$ because $4\le t-1$.
These intervals describe where $x(\tau)h(t-\tau)$ can be nonzero in each time region. They are overlap intervals only; setting integral bounds and evaluating the convolution come later.

entries.lesson_core_move: Translate the overlap interval into the lower and upper $\tau$ limits for the continuous-time convolution integral.

sections.section_title: Introduction to Setting Integral Bounds from Overlap

blocks.text: At this point in the convolution setup, the supports of $x(\tau)$ and $h(t-\tau)$ have already been intersected. The result of that intersection is the overlap interval: the set of $\tau$ values where both factors can be nonzero.
The integral only accumulates product values where $x(\tau)h(t-\tau)$ can be nonzero. So once the overlap interval is known, the integral should be restricted to that interval.
The rule is direct: the left endpoint of the overlap interval becomes the lower limit of integration, and the right endpoint becomes the upper limit of integration.
This lesson is only about setting up the bounds. After the overlap has been translated into lower and upper $\tau$ limits, evaluating the integral is a separate move.

sections.section_title: Setting Bounds from a Constant Overlap Interval

example_content.example_prompt: Given that the overlap interval is $1 \le \tau \le 3$, set the bounds for the convolution integral $y(t)=\int x(\tau)h(t-\tau)\,d\tau$ on that time region.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is the given overlap interval $1 \le \tau \le 3$. This already tells us where the product $x(\tau)h(t-\tau)$ can be nonzero, so the task is only to turn those endpoints into integration bounds.
The left endpoint is $1$, so $1$ becomes the lower limit. The right endpoint is $3$, so $3$ becomes the upper limit.
The integrand stays the same because this step only changes the limits of integration. We do not evaluate the integral here.
So on this time region, the correctly bounded convolution setup is $y(t)=\int_1^3 x(\tau)h(t-\tau)\,d\tau$.

sections.section_title: Setting Bounds with a $t$-Dependent Lower Limit

example_content.example_prompt: On a time region where the overlap interval is $t-2 \le \tau \le 1$, set the bounds for the convolution integral $y(t)=\int x(\tau)h(t-\tau)\,d\tau$.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is the overlap interval $t-2 \le \tau \le 1$. Read it from left to right in the $\tau$ variable: the expression on the left is the lower endpoint, and the expression on the right is the upper endpoint.
Even though the lower endpoint contains $t$, it still becomes the lower limit. During the convolution integral, $t$ is held fixed while integration happens with respect to $\tau$.
So $t-2$ goes below the integral sign, and the constant endpoint $1$ goes above the integral sign. The integrand stays $x(\tau)h(t-\tau)$.
This is the completed bound setup for this time region. The step stops after placing the overlap endpoints as limits; it does not evaluate the integral.

sections.section_title: Setting Bounds with a $t$-Dependent Upper Limit

example_content.example_prompt: On a time region where the overlap interval is $0 \le \tau \le t+1$, set the bounds for the convolution integral $y(t)=\int x(\tau)h(t-\tau)\,d\tau$.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is the overlap interval $0 \le \tau \le t+1$. Read the interval in the order of the $\tau$ inequality: the left endpoint becomes the lower limit, and the right endpoint becomes the upper limit.
Here the lower endpoint is the constant $0$. The upper endpoint is $t+1$, and it stays in that upper-limit position even though it contains $t$.
During the convolution integral, integration is with respect to $\tau$, so $t$ is held fixed. Place $0$ below the integral sign, place $t+1$ above it, and leave the integrand unchanged.
This is the completed bound setup for this time region. The example stops at the correctly bounded convolution integral, before any evaluation.

sections.section_title: Setting Bounds When Both Limits Depend on $t$

example_content.example_prompt: On a time region where the overlap interval is $t-3 \le \tau \le t+1$, set the bounds for the convolution integral $y(t)=\int x(\tau)h(t-\tau)\,d\tau$.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is the overlap interval $t-3 \le \tau \le t+1$. Both endpoints contain $t$, but the endpoint rule is unchanged: read the interval in increasing $\tau$ order.
The expression $t-3$ is the lower endpoint because it appears on the left side of the $\tau$ inequality. The expression $t+1$ is the upper endpoint because it appears on the right side.
Since the integral is with respect to $\tau$, $t$ is held fixed while integrating. Keep both endpoint expressions in their positions, place them as the limits, and leave the integrand unchanged.
This is the correctly bounded convolution setup for this time region. Do not simplify the limits or evaluate the integral in this step.

sections.section_title: Writing Region-Specific Integrals from Overlap Bounds

example_content.example_prompt: Given the overlap intervals $0<t<1: 0\le \tau \le t$ and $1\le t<3: t-1\le \tau \le 1$, write the region-specific convolution integrals for $y(t)=\int x(\tau)h(t-\tau)\,d\tau$.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is that the overlap information is already split by time region. Treat each time region as a separate case, and apply the same endpoint-to-bounds rule inside each case.
For the first region, $0<t<1$, the overlap interval is $0\le \tau \le t$. The lower endpoint is $0$, and the upper endpoint is $t$.
For the second region, $1\le t<3$, the overlap interval is $t-1\le \tau \le 1$. The lower endpoint is $t-1$, and the upper endpoint is $1$.
Now write one convolution integral for each time region. Keep the integrand the same in both cases and change only the limits.
This is the region-specific setup. Do not merge the two regions or evaluate either integral in this step.

entries.lesson_core_move: Evaluate the convolution integral separately on each time region where the overlap bounds change, then assemble the piecewise output.

sections.section_title: Introduction to Evaluating Convolution Piece by Piece

blocks.text: In the previous convolution steps, the overlap intervals for $x(\tau)$ and $h(t-\tau)$ were already found. This lesson starts after those bounds are known. The new move is to evaluate the convolution integral separately on each time region where the overlap bounds have a fixed formula.

On one time region, the overlap gives a lower bound and an upper bound for $\tau$. Those bounds replace $-\infty$ and $\infty$ in the convolution integral. The variable of integration is $\tau$, while $t$ is treated as a fixed parameter during that regional calculation.

For each region, use the same workflow: choose the current time region, insert its bounds $L_i(t)$ and $U_i(t)$, integrate with respect to $\tau$, simplify the result as a formula in $t$, and keep the region condition attached to that formula.
The final output is not one formula produced from one set of bounds. It is a piecewise function assembled from the regional formulas, listed in the same order as the time regions.

sections.section_title: Evaluating the First Overlap Region

example_content.example_prompt: For $0 \le t \le 1$, evaluate the first-region convolution integral $y(t)=\int_0^t 1\,d\tau$.

explanation_blocks.text: The current time region is $0 \le t \le 1$. On this region, the overlap bounds have already been found: $0 \le \tau \le t$. The task is only to evaluate the regional integral and keep the time condition attached.
The integration variable is $\tau$, so $t$ is treated as fixed while we take the antiderivative.
Now substitute the upper bound $t$ and the lower bound $0$.
So the first overlap region contributes the regional formula $y(t)=t$ for $0 \le t \le 1$. This is the first piece, not the full piecewise output.

sections.section_title: Evaluating a Middle Region with New Bounds

example_content.example_prompt: For $1 \le t \le 2$, evaluate the middle-region convolution integral $y(t)=\int_0^1 1\,d\tau$.

explanation_blocks.text: The current time region is $1 \le t \le 2$. The cue is that this is a middle region, so the bounds are not inherited from the first region. Here the overlap bounds are fixed: $0 \le \tau \le 1$.
The integration variable is still $\tau$. Since the integrand is constant and the bounds are fixed, this regional value will be constant on the whole interval.
Now substitute the fixed upper bound $1$ and lower bound $0$.
So the middle overlap region contributes the regional value $y(t)=1$ for $1 \le t \le 2$. The method stayed the same; the bounds changed.

sections.section_title: Evaluating the Last Overlap Region

example_content.example_prompt: For $2 \le t \le 3$, evaluate the last-region convolution integral $y(t)=\int_{t-2}^1 1\,d\tau$.

explanation_blocks.text: The current time region is $2 \le t \le 3$. The cue is that this is the last nonzero overlap region, so the overlap is shrinking. The lower bound now depends on $t$: $t-2 \le \tau \le 1$.
The integration variable is still $\tau$, so $t$ is treated as fixed while we take the antiderivative.
Now substitute upper minus lower carefully. The upper bound is $1$, and the lower bound is $t-2$.
So the last overlap region contributes the regional formula $y(t)=3-t$ for $2 \le t \le 3$. The result decreases because the lower bound moves upward as $t$ increases.

sections.section_title: Assembling the Piecewise Convolution Output

example_content.example_prompt: Given $y(t)=t$ for $0 \le t \le 1$, $y(t)=1$ for $1 \le t \le 2$, and $y(t)=3-t$ for $2 \le t \le 3$, assemble the nonzero piecewise convolution output.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is that the regional formulas have already been evaluated. The task is not to integrate again; it is to preserve each formula with its own time interval and list the pieces in increasing order of $t$.
Now place those three formula-interval pairs under one piecewise definition for $y(t)$.

This is the nonzero piecewise convolution output. The formulas stay attached to their original intervals, and no outside zero-output regions are added because the prompt asks only for the nonzero overlap pieces.

entries.lesson_core_move: Identify values of $t$ where the supports of $x(\tau)$ and $h(t-\tau)$ do not overlap, and set the convolution output to zero on those regions.

sections.section_title: Introduction to Recognizing No-Overlap Regions

blocks.text: In a convolution, the integral only accumulates values of $\tau$ where both factors are nonzero. If the support of $x(\tau)$ and the support of $h(t-\tau)$ do not overlap, then the product $x(\tau)h(t-\tau)$ is zero for every $\tau$, so the convolution output is zero for that value of $t$.

The two intervals to compare are the fixed support of $x(\tau)$ and the moving support of $h(t-\tau)$. The fixed support does not contain $t$. The moving support has endpoints that depend on $t$, so different values of $t$ can move it before, across, or after the fixed interval.

There are two no-overlap cases. Before contact, the moving interval is entirely to the left of the fixed interval. After contact, it is entirely to the right of the fixed interval. Each case is decided by comparing one moving endpoint with one fixed endpoint.

For a base case, suppose $x(\tau)$ is nonzero on $0\le \tau\le 2$ and $h(t-\tau)$ is nonzero on $t-1\le \tau\le t$. Before contact, the moving right endpoint $t$ is still less than $0$, so $t<0$. After contact, the moving left endpoint $t-1$ is greater than $2$, so $t>3$.
On those $t$-regions, there is no interval over which both factors are nonzero. Therefore the integrand is identically zero, and those regions become zero pieces in the final convolution output.

sections.section_title: Recognizing No Overlap Before the Moving Support Reaches $x(\tau)$

example_content.example_prompt: Suppose $x(\tau)$ is nonzero only on $1\le \tau\le 4$ and $h(t-\tau)$ is nonzero only on $t-2\le \tau\le t$. For what values of $t$ is there no overlap before the moving support reaches $x(\tau)$?

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is the phrase "before the moving support reaches $x(\tau)$." That means the moving interval for $h(t-\tau)$ is entirely to the left of the fixed interval for $x(\tau)$. For this one-sided check, compare the right endpoint of the moving support with the left endpoint of the fixed support.
The fixed support begins at $\tau=1$. The moving support ends at $\tau=t$. Before contact, that moving right endpoint must still be less than $1$.

So for every $t<1$, the interval $[t-2,t]$ lies completely to the left of $[1,4]$. There is no interval of $\tau$ where both factors are nonzero, so the convolution output is zero on that before-contact region.

sections.section_title: Recognizing No Overlap After the Moving Support Passes $x(\tau)$

example_content.example_prompt: Suppose $x(\tau)$ is nonzero only on $1\le \tau\le 4$ and $h(t-\tau)$ is nonzero only on $t-2\le \tau\le t$. For what values of $t$ is there no overlap after the moving support passes $x(\tau)$?

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is the phrase "after the moving support passes $x(\tau)$." That means the moving interval for $h(t-\tau)$ is entirely to the right of the fixed interval for $x(\tau)$. This is the opposite side from before contact, so the endpoint comparison also changes.
The fixed support ends at $\tau=4$. The moving support begins at $\tau=t-2$. After contact, that moving left endpoint must be greater than $4$.
Solving the endpoint inequality gives the after-contact $t$-region.

So for every $t>6$, the interval $[t-2,t]$ lies completely to the right of $[1,4]$. There is no interval of $\tau$ where both factors are nonzero, so the convolution output is zero on that after-contact region.

sections.section_title: Finding All Zero-Output Regions from Support Endpoints

example_content.example_prompt: Suppose $x(\tau)$ is nonzero only on $-1\le \tau\le 3$ and $h(t-\tau)$ is nonzero only on $t-2\le \tau\le t+1$. Find all $t$-regions where the convolution output is zero because the supports do not overlap.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is the word "all." We need both outside no-overlap regions: the before-contact region and the after-contact region. First record the fixed support and the moving support so each endpoint comparison is explicit.
Before contact, the moving support is entirely to the left of the fixed support. Compare the moving right endpoint $t+1$ with the fixed left endpoint $-1$.
After contact, the moving support is entirely to the right of the fixed support. Compare the moving left endpoint $t-2$ with the fixed right endpoint $3$.
These two outside regions are the complete set of no-overlap regions. On either one, there is no interval of $\tau$ where both factors are nonzero, so the convolution output is zero.

sections.section_title: Adding Zero-Output Regions to a Piecewise Convolution

example_content.example_prompt: A convolution has nonzero overlap only for $-2<t<5$, with evaluated pieces already planned for $-2<t<1$ and $1\le t<5$. Write the zero-output pieces that must be added outside the overlap region.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is that the nonzero-overlap interval is already given. Since the convolution has nonzero overlap only for $-2<t<5$, the zero-output regions are the two outside regions before and after that interval.
The region before the overlap starts is $t\le -2$. The region after the overlap ends is $t\ge 5$. On both regions, the supports do not overlap, so the convolution output is $0$.

The interior pieces should be preserved exactly as already planned. If those evaluated pieces are called $y_1(t)$ on $-2<t<1$ and $y_2(t)$ on $1\le t<5$, the zero-output regions frame them as the outer cases.
No interior formula is recomputed or moved. The only added information is that the convolution is zero outside the full nonzero-overlap interval.

entries.lesson_core_move: Apply commutativity to swap the convolution factors when doing so makes the support analysis, overlap bounds, or piecewise evaluation simpler.

sections.section_title: Introduction to Using Commutativity to Simplify Convolution

blocks.text: In a convolution integral, the usual setup is to keep one factor fixed as a function of $\tau$ and shift the other factor as a function of $t-\tau$. Then the support of the fixed factor, the support of the shifted factor, and their overlap determine the bounds for the integral.
Convolution is commutative. That means swapping the two factors does not change the output value.

The useful point is that commutativity can change the work setup. In the first form below, $x(\tau)$ is the fixed factor and $h(t-\tau)$ is the shifted factor. In the second form, $h(\tau)$ is fixed and $x(t-\tau)$ is shifted.

Use the swapped form when it makes the support work simpler. For example, if one signal has a simple finite support, it is often easier to keep that signal fixed in $\tau$ and let the other signal be the shifted factor.
Swapping is optional. The result is the same either way, so the choice is about reducing the burden of solving inequalities, finding overlap cases, or evaluating the piecewise integral.

sections.section_title: Swapping the Factors in a Convolution Integral

example_content.example_prompt: Rewrite $y(t)=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}x(\tau)h(t-\tau)\,d\tau$ using commutativity so that $h(\tau)$ is the fixed factor.

explanation_blocks.text: In the given integral, $x(\tau)$ is the fixed factor because it is written directly as a function of $\tau$. The factor $h(t-\tau)$ is the shifted factor because its argument contains $t-\tau$.
To make $h(\tau)$ the fixed factor, use commutativity and swap the roles of $x$ and $h$. The output is still $y(t)$, and $\tau$ stays the integration variable.
This is the commuted form. The value of $y(t)$ is unchanged because convolution is commutative; only the setup has changed, with $h(\tau)$ fixed and $x(t-\tau)$ shifted.

sections.section_title: Choosing the Easier Shifted Signal

example_content.example_prompt: For $x(t)=e^{-t}u(t)$ and $h(t)=u(t)-u(t-2)$, decide whether to use $\int x(\tau)h(t-\tau)\,d\tau$ or $\int h(\tau)x(t-\tau)\,d\tau$ to make the overlap setup simpler.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is the support type of each factor. The signal $x(t)=e^{-t}u(t)$ is one-sided, so its support starts at $0$ and extends to infinity. The signal $h(t)=u(t)-u(t-2)$ is a finite rectangular pulse, so its support is the interval from $0$ to $2$.
In the original order, $x(\tau)$ is fixed and $h(t-\tau)$ is shifted. That leaves the one-sided exponential as the fixed condition, but it makes the finite rectangular support move with $t$.

In the commuted order, $h(\tau)$ is fixed and $x(t-\tau)$ is shifted. Now the finite rectangular support stays as the simple fixed interval, and the shifted one-sided exponential contributes only a one-sided inequality.

Use the commuted form. It gives the same convolution value by commutativity, but it makes the overlap setup simpler because the finite interval remains fixed in $\tau$ while the one-sided exponential is the shifted factor.

sections.section_title: Setting Bounds After Swapping the Factors

example_content.example_prompt: For $x(t)=e^{-t}u(t)$ and $h(t)=u(t)-u(t-2)$, use the swapped form $\int h(\tau)x(t-\tau)\,d\tau$ to set the integration bounds for $0<t<2$.

explanation_blocks.text: Use the swapped order chosen in the previous section. In this order, $h(\tau)$ is the fixed factor and $x(t-\tau)$ is the shifted factor.
The rectangular pulse $h(t)=u(t)-u(t-2)$ is nonzero from $0$ to $2$. Since it is fixed as $h(\tau)$, this gives the fixed support condition in the integration variable.
The exponential factor is one-sided: $x(u)=e^{-u}u(u)$ is nonzero when $u\ge 0$. In the shifted factor $x(t-\tau)$, replace $u$ with $t-\tau$ and solve for $\tau$.
Now intersect the fixed support with the shifted support condition. Before using the stated time region, the allowed $\tau$ values must satisfy both constraints.
On the region $0<t<2$, the value of $t$ lies inside the fixed interval $[0,2]$. Therefore the overlap starts at $0$ and ends at $t$.
So for $0<t<2$, the lower integration bound is $0$ and the upper integration bound is $t$. This sets up the integral; evaluation comes after the bounds are known.

sections.section_title: Evaluating the Simpler Piecewise Convolution

example_content.example_prompt: Use commutativity to compute $y(t)=(x*h)(t)$ for $x(t)=e^{-t}u(t)$ and $h(t)=u(t)-u(t-2)$, giving the answer as a piecewise function of t.

explanation_blocks.text: Use the commuted form so the rectangular pulse stays fixed in $\tau$. Since $h(\tau)$ is nonzero on $0\le \tau\le 2$ and $x(t-\tau)$ is nonzero when $t-\tau\ge 0$, the shifted exponential contributes the condition $\tau\le t$.
These two support conditions split the calculation into three regions. For $t<0$, the condition $\tau\le t$ lies entirely to the left of the fixed interval $[0,2]$, so there is no overlap.
For $0\le t<2$, the overlap runs from $0$ up to $t$. On this interval, $h(\tau)=1$ and $x(t-\tau)=e^{-(t-\tau)}$, so the integral is evaluated with bounds $0$ to $t$.
For $t\ge 2$, the condition $\tau\le t$ includes the entire fixed interval $[0,2]$. The overlap is the full rectangular-pulse interval, so the bounds are $0$ to $2$.
Assemble the three regional results into one piecewise output. The two nonzero formulas agree at $t=2$ because both give $1-e^{-2}$ there.
